utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we resume the examination of Witness DP17, I can now confirm to you that we will not sit on the 11th, the 12th and the 13th of December. That means we will only sit on Monday and Tuesday next week. Then, Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. DP17, may I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have made at the beginning of your testimony. Before you will be examined by counsel for the Prosecution, I'd like to ask you one question, but I would rather do that in private session. Could we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session again. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please assist because the ELMO is obstructing the view. If you could please remove it. Yes. Thank you. It is the upper part that is...

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you lower the mirror part, is that possible? We will make do, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, when you held this position, what was your rank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I entered the war with the rank of sergeant and I think that at the time when I was carrying out this duty I held the rank of second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So to the best of your recollection during the time that you held this post you were an officer in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the time period when you held this duty from the end of 1992 until May or June 1993, did you have an office, and if so, where was that office located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had an office and it was located at the command of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you refresh my recollection, Witness, as to where the brigade headquarters was located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was located at the Velika Aleja or the great alley, and it was the so-called villa of Sipad company. It was Velika Aleja at Ilidza, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps there is a problem of interpretation, but I don't think it's useful to correct it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question, Witness: Having been trained as a lawyer, did you have any specific functions regarding legal issues during the time that you held this post?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see yesterday I clearly said that I completed the first degree of the law school which means that I didn't complete the entire degree. So I couldn't be a lawyer. According to our regulations you have to finish the entire -- all the years of law school or four years of the school. And you also have to pass a special exam in order to be a practising lawyer. So I wasn't a lawyer in that sense. I couldn't be.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [redacted] So that's why I had to explain that I couldn't even theoretically be a lawyer, that's what I wanted to clear up. But certainly there were legal matters, of course, except that we also had administrative assistants, associates, so to speak. These were officials at this post and they also carried out duties that you are mentioning. These are legal matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What kind of legal matters did you deal with during the time period from late 1992 through May of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said clearly and I listed the duties that I carried out. Very few purely legal matters. My job was to gather information about the morale in the brigade, and I can repeat so that there is no dilemma. Cooperation with religious dignitaries on the local level, and I said mostly during the Serb Orthodox holidays, and I also said that unfortunately my post also included carrying out duties in relation to funerals and providing accommodation for these families as much as we were able to. And I can be more specific, and it is also going to funerals, going to express condolences and so on, and also cooperation with the local newspaper and the local radio station in relation to these duties to do with the morale in the unit that I belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I understand that aspect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask to turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is confirmed on my screen, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, did your duties include any kind of disciplinary issues such as those that might affect the front lines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it included cooperation with the Military Police whose duty it was to provide security and, perhaps, although we didn't really have such cases, they had to respond to failure to go to the line to the combat line, to go to the trenches, to go to guard posts. They had to prevent trafficking, if such phenomena appeared that had to do with selling cigarettes, cars. Special attention was paid to preventing alcohol from being consumed to preventing trafficking. If there was such situations, well, these weren't desirable situations. So, in that sense, there was such cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I assume, Witness, that you regularly attended brigade staff meetings, that such meetings were held on a regular basis; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I wasn't absent, naturally. If I was there, if I was present, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall at any time during the period from September 1992 through August 1994 being present at any of these staff meetings when reports concerning orders violations were discussed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was such situations, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What kind of orders violations do you recall being discussed during this time period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were situations when it was necessary -- well, for example, I will provide you with an example. They attempted to not to have two brothers in the same trench or father and a son in the same trench. And on the other hand, these people wanted to be together in the one trench. I don't know if I have mentioned this, but our brigade launched decisive defence. We didn't have the right to withdraw because right behind our lines there was the urban part of Serbian Ilidza and our women and children were there. So people would sleep in the trenches. Yesterday, I said about 90 -- when I mentioned 90 per cent combat readiness yesterday, you probably -- you can probably understand this, that this means that men are engaged all the time. So because of that specific situation, since there was constant danger of the trenches being hit and of men being killed, the command's position was rational. They didn't want two brothers to go to the same trench or a father and a son to go to the same trench. But there were such situations when this happened and in a few of those situations you know you put men in different trenches and different shifts, but they would then appear and insist on doing the opposite, not respecting that order. They wanted to be together. So there was such situations and we dealt with them through discussions. We didn't penalise this or rather the brigade commander usually didn't punish this. But there were discussions about this at the brigade command. Other discussions, for example, concerned conditions obtained for a soldier to be and visit his family. We weren't all from Ilidza. There were men, there were soldiers who on the other side about 5 kilometres as the crow flies. But when the airport was handed over to the French UNPROFOR forces for their use, it was closed for us too. And then it was necessary to cover 100 kilometres to get to the Serb -- to the eastern part of Serbian Ilidza. There was people from Pale, from Sokolac, there were people from Herzegovina, from Krajina. So you had to allow these people to visit their families after a few months. Sometimes this would happen a little late. But in that case, the command would discuss, if people returned late, two, three or five days late. In such cases, the commander had to take appropriate measures, mete out the appropriate punishment. So there was discussions at such meetings. I was also present when the men -- when they had leave, when they went home, they would drink and then, as is often the case, there would be unruly behaviour. So we would meet and discuss these things. There were other such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you told us yesterday that you -- that your brigade was under orders to only fire at individuals bearing arms; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At any time from September 1992 through August 1994, do you recall any discussions at staff meetings of your brigade in which there were discussions concerning violations of that order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember talking about violations, but I know that they always emphasised that this should be respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So what you are telling us is that you are unaware of anyone -- of any discussions concerning anyone violating that order within your brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At any time from September 1992 through August 1994 do you recall having any dealings or interactions with a Military Prosecutor concerning someone violating that order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday you told us that tanks fired on Ilidza and you said "our observers reported this." Do you know if this incident or incidents involving ABiH tank fire on Ilidza was reported to the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was reported to the observers we mentioned yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Who made the report? Who from your brigade made the report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was even a direct telephone line and a radio link, Motorolas we used, and the brigade commander was responsible for this. This was his field of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did the brigade commander report this directly to the UN and if so to whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to the observers with whom he had a -- to whom he had a telephone and radio link. And we also had regular reports, regular contact. You are asking me just about the UN forces now. So it was for the UN force whose were at the airport and the observers that I mentioned yesterday. So there was a direct telephone line and a radio link, a Motorola link, And also through written reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was the Motorola radio link a field-type radio, a portable radio, or was it a radio that sat on a desk at the brigade headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were Motorolas, mobile devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: They were hand-held walkie-talkie type radios; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How many personnel in your brigade had one of these Motorola radios that could be used to communicate with the UN?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the commander and we had an officer for communications and for contact with UNPROFOR. So he was the other person who had direct link to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But there were two people, is that what you are telling us, the commander and the communications officer, both had Motorola hand-held radios to communicate with the UN?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall if the commander carried that Motorola radio with him at all times or at those times when you saw the commander, did he have that Motorola radio with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the time, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you, on those occasions when you were with the commander, could you hear the UN communications taking place on the radio as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean between us or the commander of the brigade, the commander of the brigade and the UNPROFOR members or the UNPROFOR members among themselves? The interpretation I received said that it concerned UNPROFOR members talking among themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Actually, both. Let's start with the first situation. I assume that if the UN was attempting to contact the brigade commander that you would be able to hear that on the radio that the brigade commander had with him; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's logical, if I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could you also hear communications between the UN officers, perhaps speaking amongst themselves in English or French or some other language, could you also hear them speaking between themselves on the radio that your commander had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that would have been difficult. I think that in general it is practically something that is difficult, but I never heard such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: To your recollection you never heard any languages being spoken on the UN Motorolas or the Motorolas that you had, other than when they were trying to communicate with your brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You also mentioned a landline telephone that was available. Was that a regular telephone where the brigade commander or communications commander would pick up the phone and dial a number, or was it a direct line where the commander or communications officer would simply pick up the phone and someone on the other end would automatically answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a line that was used -- it was an existing telephone line that was used so it was used for regular telephone communication before the war. And that line was used as a direct telephone line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know when the brigade commander or communications officer was using that phone to speak to the UN, do you know the physical location of the person that they were speaking to within the UN? Do you know where that person was that they were calling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you told us yesterday about the location of four United Nations' observations posts within the area of responsibility of your brigade, including one that you said was right in front of the command. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, about 100 metres in front of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know if these were simply observation posts or were these some kind of checkpoints or checkposts that were manned by UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the one you've asked me about, it was just an observation post because there weren't any streets there, there were no cross-roads, so there was no place where they could have put a checkpoint up, no place where they could have carried out controls.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: From the position of your headquarters, your brigade headquarters, could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask for a clarification, Mr. Mundis. Your question was about four observation posts, and then in the answer I read that the witness said "the one you asked me about," and since I had in mind that you asked about four, I -- unless the witness when he said "about 100 metres in front of the command" but it is my recollection, but unfortunately I cannot consult yesterday's transcript. He told us about four approximately 100 metres in front of the command or is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I can clarify it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday you told us that there were four UN posts, observation posts within the area of responsibility of your brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you told us that one of those four posts was approximately 100 metres away from your brigade headquarters; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 100 metres, and that's the one that you asked me about, so I answered the question about that. The question was about whether it was an observation post or an observation post and a checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Precisely. Now, let's focus now on the one that was near the brigade headquarters which you said was an observation post but not a checkpoint because there weren't any streets there. From the brigade headquarters, were you able to observe what the UN personnel in that observation post were doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean directly from the facility where the brigade was located? You want to know whether we could see what they were doing when they were observing; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In general. If you were either coming to the brigade headquarters or departing the brigade headquarters or standing in front of the brigade headquarters or behind the brigade headquarters or beside it, could you see that observation post from the brigade headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. When I was coming to the brigade command, it would be true to say that we could see it. It was -- I will describe it for you. It was made of sandbags. There was a large space. And when the doors opened, let's call it a door, the entrance to the area, there was no obstruction to one's view. We could see that there was someone with a pair of binoculars observing to the left and to the right. Because our line could be seen from that part, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall whether there were usually or regularly any kind of white UN marked vehicles parked next to or in the immediate vicinity of this observation post?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can remember that in the vicinity, they were parked in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What kind of vehicles were there, UN vehicles were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were mostly personnel carriers produced in France. I think it was by Renault. They were white. There were large vehicles and small vehicles. We called the small ones zaba, that is to say frogs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you know the nationality of the UN forces that were at this checkpoint or this observation post, excuse me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were from France.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, in your own mind did you make a distinction between the various United Nations' forces that were present in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. You could distinguish them on the basis of the flags that they had, their national flags. That was the first visual sign that you could observe. And when you had contact with them, naturally it was always clear on their uniforms. In addition to the UN sign they had the sign of the country that they came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall the dates that this observation post existed, 100 meters from the brigade headquarters? Do you recall the -- approximately the first time you saw it and approximately the last time you saw it there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember when I saw it for the first time. If we are talking about the period of time, I think it was there for over a year, but when exactly I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know if these UN forces that were near the brigade headquarters, were they part of UNPROFOR or were they United Nations Military Observers or did you not make a distinction in your own mind between those two categories of UN personnel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were United Nations' observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know if the other three posts that were within your brigade's area of responsibility were posts manned by UNPROFOR or by United Nations Military Observers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't say for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At any of these four posts within your brigade's area of responsibility, did you ever personally speak to any of these UN personnel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, I did. I had the opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What kind of the issues did you discuss with these UN personnel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically the observation post which was there, and of course the observers, the observers, as you say were there, since there was the observation post. And one day they said they wanted me to go with them to their observation post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, was --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was -- that's about the observation post you've asked me about. And I can tell you specifically about the one in Nedzarici, if that is part of the answer. So, yes, I did speak to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall on how many occasions you spoke to the UN personnel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say precisely, but there were such talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were all of the UN personnel that you dealt with within your brigade's area of responsibility French or were there any UN personnel in your brigade's area of responsibility of another nationality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from members who were French, there were also Ukrainian members, UN members in the area of responsibility of our brigade. Although, it did happen that there were also some Spanish UN soldiers who came, but those that we are speaking about, those were stationed there were mostly French or Ukrainian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the names or ranks of any of the French or Ukrainian UN personnel that you spoke with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember Captain Desvouges [phoen] specifically, he was French. And yes I remember that there were also Dutch soldiers. There was one lieutenant-colonel I remember who happened to be there. He was lieutenant-colonel from Holland, and he happened to be there on our Orthodox Christmas. He celebrated with us on that day. He wanted to go to the line with us, that was on the 7th of January 1994. There were also English soldiers, but I don't recall any names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, were there ever any occasions when you personally were sent by the brigade commander to lodge a formal complaint with anyone from the UN?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, I didn't -- earlier I don't know whether you said or whether I clarified that we, as a brigade, for that level we had to inform the liaison officer at the corps in case there were any protests, any complaints, if that's what you mean, where there would be our liaison officer at the corps, and he would react, he would deal with it. So I -- I didn't quite understand because why would a commander, if he had a -- if he had a liaison officer and that was his area of expertise, why would he want me to do something, and he wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, who was the liaison officer at the corps level that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was Mr. Indjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were any complaints that your brigade would have had funneled through that individual?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, I did not. For the commander, I don't know. As far as this gentleman is concerned, I know that he was there and I've even seen him on a couple of occasions. But specifically I never had contacts with him because, again I reiterate, this was the area of responsibility of the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So, Witness, what you are telling us is that no time did you ever personally report any formal complaints to any member of any UN command in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you'll allow me, I'd like to clarify something here. When persons happen to be there, members of UNPROFOR forces, if they happen to be there, and if then there was firing at that time, specifically when there was a truce that was agreed or signed, well then I cannot rule out the possibility that I didn't say to them, "the Muslim side is firing on our positions or on Ilidza," or perhaps I may have said, "can't you see what is happening." So I cannot rule out the possibility that I did not have the opportunity to say this and to report myself, as well. But when we are talking about official contact, I told you who was in charge of that, and that was the brigade commander. So there were also these kind of situations. When I would find myself in a situation when it would be not be logical if I was sitting there and I was observing this, and then it would be illogical for me not to tell them, "can't you see what they are doing." So that would be the answer to that question, as it was -- as it was interpreted to me, your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Did you ever personally receive any reports from any military officer within the United Nations concerning allegations that members of your brigade were intentionally sniping at civilians; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever personally receive any reports from any military officer within the United Nations concerning allegations that forces from your brigade were intentionally shelling civilians; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was the topic of United Nations' complaints about sniping of civilians ever brought up at any staff meeting that you attended; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please answer that question, Mr. DP17. The question was whether the topic of United Nations' complaints about the sniping of civilians were ever brought up at any staff meeting that you attended? Was it or was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in a sense that -- well, perhaps you could clarify the question. Mr. President, I'd like to ask the Prosecutor if he can just clarify this question a little bit. What I mean is, first of all, we didn't have snipers, so I don't understand that we could have discussed something which we didn't have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is the reason why I repeated the question. The question is whether any complaint from the United Nations about sniping. You are not asked to confirm whether there was any sniping. But whether ever a complaint of the United Nations about sniping was discussed during a meeting you attended, any staff meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You've talked about -- Witness, you told us that on several occasions you were at the corps, you saw the accused, General Galic, and that on about ten occasions he was at your brigade headquarters. At any time when the accused, General Galic, was present, was the topic of United Nations' complaints about the sniping of civilians ever discussed; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On how many occasions, to the best of your recollection, was that the topic of discussion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to -- I have to -- evidently I have to clarify this. There was, in a sense, that the Muslims -- and I recall this extremely well -- that the Muslims reported that somebody was firing. And then the general would order that there shouldn't be any firing, absolutely no firing on civilians. And I said that yesterday and I stand by that. That every time when we met this order was reiterated. Independently, whether there was a report in this sense, the one report that you are mentioning, but in any case it was always stressed that attention has to be paid and we did pay attention and that is how we forwarded this, that civilians were not to be targeted while it was logical to fire on Muslim soldiers on the other side. It was war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, let me repeat the question: On how many occasions to the best of your recollection, was that the topic of discussion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that at least once we discussed this. And I think it would be arbitrary for me to say that I can't remember if you would ask me about the date, but there were such discussions. There were such discussions and I said, more or less, how these discussions went. There was an exclusive ban, and on the other hand, we didn't fire on civilians, and it was never said directly that UNPROFOR forces had ever seen anything, but it was always that the other side had told them and then they would, of course -- would then report through this way that was done on the local level, what we've already discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you've said this discussion occurred at least once. Do you -- you be more specific how many times do you remember having this discussion with the accused?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said at least once it was said, but every time when we had discussions it was ordered by the general to all those who are present at these reporting meetings, it was always stressed that civilians were not to be targeted, that civilian facilities were not to be targeted. And now it was -- I have to say it was very hard for us. You know the situation, if you followed it. I said yesterday if you know, you'll probably know, all our lines, our positions were on a flat piece of land in a valley. All our houses were either on ground floor level or one-storey buildings. So it was difficult to break these ceasefires any, to violate them. So it was always our complaints that we -- we had to make. How were they making up these complaints, I don't know. I know that the general, Stanislav Galic, every occasion whenever we met he availed himself of that opportunity to warn how important it was to respect Geneva Conventions. And if I have to reiterate it again, I will, that civilians should not be targeted, should not be fired on, that cultural and religious facilities should not be fired on. And all this I have already told you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you've told us that you met with General Galic on three or four occasions at the corps. By that I take it you mean at the corps headquarters at Lukavica Barracks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you've told us that on approximately ten occasions, General Galic came to the brigade headquarters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least ten times, more than ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So what you're telling us is that on each of these at least 13 or 14 occasions, General Galic discussed with you complaints that he had received from the ABiH -- from the UN about sniping of civilians?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if this could be done perhaps in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I take it that it is better to do so. Madam Usher, could I please ask you to escort the witness for one second out of the courtroom, Mr. DP17. Mr. Mundis, you reflected the words of the witness by saying that "so what you are telling us then is that on each of these at least 13 or 14 occasions, General Galic had discussed with you complaints that he had received from the ABiH." It is my recollection - I don't know whether the objection was about that - that at all these occasions he repeated his orders, let me say it short, fire at civilians, but then only at least on one occasion but the witness was not clear on whether it occurred more than once. At least more than one occasion the discussion found its origin in a complaint.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. President. I can rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so. Madam Usher, could you please -- or is there any other?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that was perfect, Mr. President, as always.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. You may proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, let me rephrase the question. You've told us that on at least 13 or 14 occasions General Galic repeated his order that civilians were not to be targeted by snipers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that was a leading question. I -- what I wanted is precisely to comment on this. I didn't say this like this. And the only thing I said was that I recall, I know, and this has to be clearly recorded, that these -- at these meetings what was always stressed, which is logical for us and normal for us, that firing is not to be done. I didn't mention sniping. And General Galic never told us not to fire from snipers, because we never had any snipers. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, the witness corrected himself, but may I add to it that where specific attention was drawn to the answers given by the witness until then, I would have expected not a -- that you would have not put something to the witness that he had not said until that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I apologise for that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, was the topic of UN complaints about shelling of civilians ever brought up at any staff meeting that you attended?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are speaking about the shelling now. I don't recall that there was a discussion regarding this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any discussion about the issue of UN complaints about shelling ever being brought up in your presence, whether at a staff meeting, in a meeting with the accused or at any other meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember. I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall ever receiving or having discussions about receiving information from the corps liaison officer about complaints concerning the targeting of civilians on the ABiH side of the line, and that the shooters involved were in areas under the control of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember such a situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall at any time when you were attending staff meetings any information being discussed about reports coming from the liaison officer at Lukavica Barracks concerning any subject?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that. You've practically asked me the same question twice. I am saying again, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Are you aware of any investigations conducted by your brigade or any of its personnel concerning allegations that forces in the brigade were targeting civilians on the other side of the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was never an investigation of this nature, nor do I remember any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the time that you had discussions with the accused about the UN reports that individuals were targeted, did the accused at any time direct your brigade commander to conduct an investigation?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I ask the Prosecution to clarify on which side, by which side were individuals targeted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, let me say two things: First, Mr. Mundis, it will be clear to you that the -- that this is a difference between the Prosecution and Defence case, and, therefore, it would be good always to be quite clear on that. On the other hand, I take it, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that where Mr. Mundis specified this several times in his question that not without giving prior notice he would change that position, so that there would hardly be any chance of confusion, at least chance being so small that the witness certainly would have drawn our attention to similar confusion. I think it is time for a break, but perhaps we first ask the witness to answer the last question. The last question was and I complete it now, that whether you had at any time discussions with General Galic about UN reports that individuals on the BiH side were targeted, that when at the time you had such discussions, whether General Galic at any time directed your brigade commander to conduct an investigation. So was there ever an investigation ordered to the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we will have a break. I was not very clear, Mr. Mundis, when I said that the witness corrected himself. That could be understood in two different ways, is that he himself corrected without specification who he corrected. What I should have said is that the witness himself corrected you. We will adjourn until a quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, please escort the witness into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to draw your attention to those occasions when you were present with meetings with the accused at Lukavica Barracks. You've told us that there were three or four such meetings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was the purpose of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main purpose of the meetings was to report on the situation in our brigade. And this reporting also involved reporting on the security situation, morale in the brigade, logistics, intelligence on enemy activity in the zone defended by our brigade. This was the main purpose of those meetings. Those were the most crucial issues in wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate time period when these meetings took place, perhaps the month and year, if you don't recall the dates?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was during the period we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You can't be more specific with respect to month and year when these meetings took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in 1993 and in 1994. Those are the years concerned. So it was in during that period, 1993, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to ask if you recall who was present at these meetings, and in order to save time by not going into private session, if you can simply give us the titles of the persons that you recall being present at that meeting, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were people from the command of other brigades in the corps. Those people were present. It is difficult for me to remember exactly. They had various ranks, from that of captain up to that of major, or lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was your brigade commander present at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was there, too, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall if any of the battalion commanders from your brigade were present at the meeting or meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any such meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall if all of the --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. If you would allow me, I'd like to clarify this. We are only talking about meetings in the corps command?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In that case, I don't remember battalion commanders being present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall whether commanders, the commanders of the other battalions in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps were present at these meetings as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned some ten "inspections," was the word you used yesterday, of the brigade which were carried out by the accused. Do you know during which time period these inspections occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was also in 1993 and 1994, that was the period concerned, and in 1992, at the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were these inspections carried out over a regular interval, such as every two to three months, the Corps Commander would come to the brigade, or were they bunched so that the ten inspections came in a shorter period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't talk about the plan now. Mr. General -- General Galic would be able to tell you about that, but it was a long time ago. But as you said a minute ago, there were perhaps intervals of a month or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So it would be fair to say that General Galic came to the brigade headquarters every month or two and conducted one of these inspections; is that a fair characterisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What exactly did these inspections entail?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would visit individual lines, front lines, and they entailed discussions that I have already mentioned, reports that command brigade submitting reports that I have mentioned. I wouldn't want to repeat myself. That is what it involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say "they would visit individual lines, front lines" are you telling us that General Galic visited the front lines in the area of responsibility of the Ilidza Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you personally accompany General Galic on any of these visits to the front lines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I personally had the opportunity of accompanying him on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall on the occasion that you accompanied him, which part or parts of the front line you visited?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we visited the north-eastern part of our line. I apologise. I have to correct myself. On two occasions I have just remembered. Once it was the south-western part, that is the part on the slope of Igman, I personally accompanied him. And on one occasion, it was the north-eastern side, that's our line in the direction of the river of Dobrinja. That's where we were together, in those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Based on your duties and responsibilities in the period after May 1993, did you ever take any special precautions during those times when General Galic visited the front lines of the Ilidza Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, General Galic didn't allow any special measures to be taken, any security measures. He felt safe among his men, among his soldiers, so that there weren't any particular measures, security measures that were taken. I don't remember any such measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know or did you receive any reports or information about whether General Galic visited the School for the Blind on any of these visits to the brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know if during any of these visits General Galic visited the School of Theology or the convent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know during the time periods when or those times when General Galic visited the brigade, if he inspected or reviewed the brigade's reports or documents or files or any of the materials that you may have had in the brigade headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of him personally examining documents. I wasn't present. I don't remember seeing him personally examining documents, going through documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know from any discussions that you may have had with anyone about whether General Galic conducted similar inspections of other brigades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say that I saw that, but one would expect that he did visit other brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever have any discussions with General Galic or anyone else that led you to conclude that General Galic had visited the front lines in other brigades' area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he did. And as far as I know, but again it is difficult to remember, I think he did and I also had information according to which he did visit other brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you be more specific or elaborate upon this other information that you had which led you to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when speaking to colleagues from those brigades, from commands brigade -- the brigade commands, when speaking to these people, I obtained the information that I have just told you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the specifics of what was discussed with your colleagues from other brigades? Do you recall anything that they told you or any specific places where they might have taken the accused when he visited their brigades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the places, it wouldn't be appropriate now to say where someone took the General or to say where the General went because that was a matter for that brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. DP17, if you know, please answer the question. If you don't know, of course, you can't answer the question. But if you know where he was taken or where he went when visiting other brigades, please tell us and if you don't know, please tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I really don't know. I don't know the exact places.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, based on your experience and your dealings with the accused, did it seem to you that he was the type of commander that one could characterise as a hands-on commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did it seem to you that he had a good sense of what was going on around the front lines of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am convinced that he was very familiar with the situation in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, to your knowledge did there ever come a time when the accused set up some kind of command post for the corps within the Ilidza Brigade's area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You don't remember any kind of forward command post or any kind of corps level command post in your brigade's area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no forward command post in the zone of responsibility of our brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you told us earlier that on numerous occasions the accused made it clear that civilians were not to be targeted; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you regard that as a -- as an order coming from the command, from the Corps Commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly, among other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you regard this order as being of the type of order that military people would refer to as a standing order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And by the term "standing order" within military circles, what that means is an order that is in effect indefinitely until it is rescinded; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, orders are usually in force until they are revoked. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 16821 to 16827.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What does the term "standing order" mean to you, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for an example, if I am ordered to march 20 kilometres, I will do so and then I will wait for another order, or I will wait until this order is changed and I am told to return back or to continue. That would be a specific example. That is what you wanted, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, actually, the type of examples that you just gave might not be standing orders. Let me put it a different way. If you are ordered to march 20 kilometres and you march 20 kilometres, that order has been carried out, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could also -- you could consider it to have been carried out, but the question is what is the task. Because there -- several orders can be included in one task, isn't that right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely. But if the order is for you to march 20 kilometres and you, in fact, march 20 kilometres, then that order is carried out and that order in effect is extinguished because you carried out the task you were ordered to do; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: A standing order by distinction would be an order such as "I am ordering you to keep your barracks room clean." That's an order that even though you cleaned the barracks room on Monday, you still have to clean it on Tuesday, and on Wednesday and on Thursday. And the fact that you cleaned it once, doesn't have any bearing at all on the order because it is an order for you to do something over and over and over again; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So the order that you received from General Galic not to target civilians on the other side of the confrontation line was a standing order in the sense that you were to follow that order every single day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, clearly. That's very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever hear or read any reports that this order of the Corps Commander was violated by any of the forces within the Ilidza Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If the order was not violated, Witness, do you have any idea or explanation as to why it was necessary to keep repeating this order, given that it was a standing order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you took the example of cleaning up a room, but there is always someone there to control that and to make sure that the area is cleaned. And one would expect that General Galic, given his position, was in a situation which he could control that and insist on what we have been talking about. So as we said, that wasn't his only role. That wasn't the only thing that he told us, if we are referring to the meetings at which I was present. Mr. Prosecutor, this is the impression I am gaining, it seems as if the General only repeated what you are insisting on at all of these meetings. So one gains the impression that all he said was that one should not fire at civilians. I have told you what --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, let me try the question once again. If the order was not violated, what was the need to keep repeating the order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will answer that question by providing you another example, it has to do with cleaning weapons. You order the men to maintain their weapons, to clean them, and it is a standing order, and this concerns pistols, rifles, and other weapons. But it is also essential to repeat this every day, to repeat this order that weapons have to be cleaned. I think this answer should be sufficiently clear for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, based on the staff work that you participated in within your brigade, were you familiar with the locations of your brigade's artillery and mortar assets during the period from September 1992 through August 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did your brigade have mortars on the grounds of the convent during that period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the grounds of the convent, as far as I know it didn't have any mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At any period between September 1992 and August 1994, the Ilidza Brigade had no mortars of any kind on the grounds of the convent; is that what you are telling us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At any time between September 1992 and August 1994 did the Ilidza Brigade have any mortars deployed on the grounds of the School of Theology?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At any time between September 1992 and August 1994 did the Ilidza Brigade have any mortars deployed at the barracks near Stupsko Brdo?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object. I have to say that I am lost a little bit. Could the witness perhaps take his headphones off?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you first tell us in more abstract terms what -- I am not quite sure whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. The problem is, abstractly speaking, bis repetita placent sed non semper et cetera. I think there is a confusion between two terms that have been used. And I don't know whether the Prosecution is using these two terms in the same sense because otherwise the same question is being asked again and I don't know that one thing that has been mentioned, I don't know whether this is the same thing that we are talking about. I hope I have been sufficiently abstract and yet clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is still not clear to me so I would like to ask the usher to -- unless there are -- Mr. Mundis you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I believe I can clarify the question in such a way that the concerns of the Defence may be alleviated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you will reformulate the question and then we will see. Please proceed. Yes, could you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, are you familiar with the barracks that are on a street named Stupsko Brdo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At any time between September 1992 and August 1994 did the Ilidza Brigade have any mortars deployed at the barracks on Stupsko Brdo Street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Nedzarici we had them, but to say that I have seen them in the barracks, I haven't. But we did have mortars. If you specifically are interested in Nedzarici, yes, we did have mortars there. Because barracks, it encompasses a couple of buildings, that's what we called "barracks."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you -- Witness, can you please elaborate upon where in Nedzarici your brigade had mortars during this time period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could approximately show you on the map where they were, from what I have seen and the locations that I have seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the assistance of the usher I ask that the witness be shown the map marked D1814, and that the witness please be provided with the pointer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to my approximate assessment, that would be about here. On one occasion I had the opportunity to see that this is where the mortars were located.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall what size the mortars were and approximately how many mortar tubes you saw at that location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we had one mortar there, 82-millimetre calibre and 120-millimetre calibre, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please take the blue felt tip marker and at the location you've indicated please mark it with the letter "A" and circle it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you told us at that location that you had one mortar there, 82-millimetre calibre and 120-millimetre calibre. By way of clarification, are you telling us that you had one 82-millimetre calibre mortar and one 120-millimetre calibre mortar, so that there were a total of two mortars there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I saw that when I saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What time period did you see those mortars there, what month or day or year did you see those mortars there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was sometime in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were those mortars kept at that location for the entire period of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, when I came there anyway, when one came to Nedzarici, anyway you couldn't just walk anywhere in Nedzarici freely, particularly people who were armed and in uniform and do that safely. Which means that when I entered Nedzarici while the battalion command was in Nedzarici and we talked about it yesterday, I would go to the battalion command or immediately I would enter the communication trenches because that was the safest way of moving about, in fact, the only safe way of moving about. And it wasn't to be expected for a mortar to be on the first front line inside the communication trench. So that's an explanation why I did not have the opportunity, one or more opportunities to see these mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The map can be returned to the Registrar. Thank you, usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, were you also aware or did you have any knowledge of any mortars being placed along Kasindolska Street between September 1992 and August 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that there were mortars along Kasindolska Street because I didn't see them, and I should have been able to see them because it would be impossible for them to be alongside Kasindolska Street because all kinds of convoys went along there. And there were observers and UNPROFOR forces. And I could clarify what you've asked. You asked me about a difference, and I couldn't remember immediately the difference between the monitors or rather the observers and the UNPROFOR forces. The main difference is that the observers or the monitors were unarmed, while the UNPROFOR forces were armed. So this is by way of completing an answer to previous question you asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Did there ever come a time when you made enquiries concerning what has been characterised as an air bomb launcher?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object, Mr. President. We are hear -- well, perhaps the witness could take off his headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The usual way is that you -- well, let's -- he has taken his earphones off. Nevertheless it is impossible that he could follow whatever has been said. So would you please try to explain first in the abstract and then see whether we can proceed this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have the impression that this goes out -- comes out of the material framework of the indictment because in relation to General Galic, there was never a question that there was an air bomb launcher. So asking questions about something which is not included in the indictment doesn't seem to be proper to us. Moreover, we don't even know about the date and I think that the Prosecution should ask a chronological question first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is whether it ever came, of course, that means within the time of the indictment. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, in order to respond I think it is more appropriate for the witness to be escorted out of the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could I ask you to escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the next line of questions that the Prosecution proposes to put to the witness do, in fact, or based on the information that we have are in fact outside of the indictment period, however, the weapons system described as an air bomb launcher is a weapons system that is completely indiscriminate. The Prosecution seeks to adduce this evidence to demonstrate the intent of this witness as a senior member of the Ilidza Brigade. The Prosecution contends that this evidence can demonstrate the intent of forces within the control and under the control of the accused with respect to seeking out this type of weapons system. The Prosecution would seek to ask this line of questions in order to demonstrate that the forces under the control of the accused may have been seeking to develop weapon systems which by their very nature, Mr. President, are indiscriminate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is about the period before or after the indictment period?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It would appear to be after the indictment period, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: After the indictment period. Is there any -- is there any clue for you to assume that these weapons were within the Sarajevo Romanija Corps during the indictment period?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we -- it would seem a bit unclear. We do have some information, but certainly the accused is not indicted for the use of this type of weapon system. The information that we do have in our possession indicates that this current witness was seeking to obtain this type of weapon system after the indictment period with respect to this accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I leave it up to your own jurisprudence and would like to remind you that you have rejected the questions that the Prosecution wanted to ask in relation to a witness who was under protective measures with relation to air bombs. And we are here exactly in the same type of situation. And the Prosecution could tell us which period afterwards are we talking about, is it end of 1995 or perhaps are we talking beginning of 1995? I don't know. And in any case, if the Prosecution has to prove the intent, the alleged intent of General Galic a posteriori, which is the only thing that they may have in their hands that can extend, because we are only looking at what we have to look at and nothing else. And also for the English booth, I think that I was badly interpreted. I have never said "et cetera." Perhaps the English booth can come to me and tell me exactly what I said what they didn't interpret. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will confer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, for your information the witness that I was referring to earlier, that was Witness AD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, the reasons you have given for putting these questions to the witness have not convinced the Chamber that this is an issue that we should for that reason hear. So no questions in that respect for this reason are allowed. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience. Thank you for your patience, Mr. DP17. Mr. Mundis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, are you familiar with the battle for Otes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your brigade took a very active part in that operation; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When did this battle take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in early December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was the objective of your forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The objective of our forces was to respond to daily shooting to the buildings that were dominant in the part. And I have to clarify here, that the locality called Peyton where Serb civilians had their accommodation and families, this locality is right next to the locality of Otes. The locality Peyton was named after low ground floor, mostly one-storey houses, from that series called the Peyton Place. And in Otes, dominant buildings were high and from those buildings on a daily basis, there was firing, shooting on to the Peyton locality. So the objective was to neutralise Muslim forces that were active, that were shooting from those buildings and were causing losses among the civilians on a daily basis, practically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I suggest to you that the operation concerning Otes in December 1992 was an SRK offensive seeking to push back the ABiH forces towards Stup; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't an offensive. You could more precisely call it as a classical type of defence, protecting of lives of civilians who were being fired on every day, every night from those buildings in relation to this locality called Peyton.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your forces -- accepting your characterisation as a classical type of defence, what your forces did was seize ground and push the ABiH back towards Stup; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The consequence of that is what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: As a result of the actions taken by the SRK forces, the ABiH was forced to withdraw with the result that its forces were in a salient with Stup in the middle of the salient; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher we ask that the witness be shown Exhibits 1312 and 1313.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: While that is being done, Witness, I have a few other questions. When was the first time you were contacted by an investigator from the Defence team of the accused?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in June this year. This was the first contact that I had with Mrs. Prodanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the substance of your discussion with Ms. Prodanovic in June of 1990 -- or June of 2002?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, mostly this was in relation to whether I would be willing to tell the truth about the war events in the area where I was and where I moved about in relation to the defence of General Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the first time when you spoke to either Ms. Pilipovic or Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the Defence lawyer whose are in the courtroom today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, and unless I am mistaken, that was August the same year, this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The usher has just brought to you the two documents that you were shown yesterday. Other than these two documents, did you at any time look at other documents with the Defence counsel prior to your testimony here in the courtroom yesterday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd like you first, Witness, to look at Defence Exhibit 1312. I'd ask you to look at the third paragraph under number 1. Do you see what I am referring to, Witness? The paragraph immediately above number 2.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Below number 2, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, no, immediately -- you see the paragraph that is numbered number "1" in effect has --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In effect that paragraph has three components to it, and the third one states "The enemy has been mainly quiet during the proceeding three or four days as far as shelling is concerned." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And that is what that sentence or phrase says, according to this document; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I heard in the Serb booth in any case that they don't have the original of the document and therefore they cannot follow. I don't know whether they can be assisted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Mr. Mundis gave us a, at least he told us that he was giving a translation of what is the first line or lines of the last part of section 1. But Mr. Mundis, I have no doubt as to your knowledge of the B/C/S language, but could we in one way or the other get the full text of that paragraph so that the Chamber can understand it. Did you prepare copies for the booth so that it could be read?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, what I was intending on doing in light of what we previously done or my understanding, is reading a couple of sentences of this document to the witness and putting it to the witness in that form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that suggests -- but then it would not be better to ask the witness to read it in the original language so that immediately we have a check on the correctness of your translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely, we can do that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps then would you please invite the witness to read slowly the part you are interested in. The only part I can follow is three to 4.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. President, could it be put on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if the text could be put on the ELMO so that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I take it that yesterday no copy was provided to the interpreters, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then could it -- it is on the ELMO, I take it. Could it be zoomed in on the last part of -- is that visible for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I then ask the witness to slowly read where it starts with at least the letters N-A-P-A-R-I-J-A, so that part, yes, could you please read that very slowly. It could be -- yes, please leave it on the ELMO. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Over the last three or four days the enemy was mainly calm as far as shelling is concerned. But today in the course of the day, he showed his real face, and thus, in addition to the material damage done, he put the lives of people in danger. Fortunately, no one was killed and no one was seriously wounded."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. DP17. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, can you please look down to paragraph 5 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could it be moved on the ELMO so that paragraph 5 can be read.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please read what is indicated in paragraph 5, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17 [Resumed]
